unit-sgt2.source: Study Guide for Test 2, imported as issued

summary.text: The class Study Guide for Test 2, question for question — piecewise-defined functions and absolute value, step functions, arithmetic sequences (recursive and explicit), arithmetic series and sigma notation, solving absolute-value equations, and a quadratic inequality solved by graphing. This unit is the GRADER for your paper pass: work the printout first, then enter your answers here, untimed. Question numbers match the paper.

why.text: Doing the guide on paper is the real rehearsal — the test is on paper too. Entering your answers here afterward does two things paper can't: it grades you instantly with a walkthrough on every miss, and it quietly files each miss into the Growth Zone so the exact skills you dropped come back for another pass before Test 2.

objectives.text: Evaluate and graph piecewise-defined functions, including absolute value written as a piecewise rule.
Read a step function's domain, range, minimum and maximum from a table.
Move between the recursive and explicit definitions of an arithmetic sequence, and find any term.
Write and evaluate an arithmetic series in sigma notation, and find its sum.
Solve an absolute-value equation by splitting it into two cases, and solve a quadratic inequality by finding its boundary points.

parentNote.text: Imported AS ISSUED, same approach as the Test 1 Study Guide — paper first, app as grader. All 30 answers were independently re-derived (arithmetic, sigma notation, sums, the absolute-value equation, the quadratic inequality) and matched the teacher's key exactly on every question. Five questions had to be adapted because their paper answer is a graph or a written explanation the app can't reproduce or grade (1, 2, 4, 16, 22): each now asks for the underlying number or rule instead, testing the same skill, and is marked as a study suggestion rather than straight from the source. This file (ExamView - Alg 2 Study Guide Test 2.pdf) sits in the same Drive folder as the Topic 2 (quadratics) lesson PDFs, but its actual content — piecewise functions and arithmetic sequences/series — is Topic 1 material, not Topic 2, so it shelves here rather than under Topic 2.

nextUp.text: Print or open the paper guide, work it fully, then come back and enter your answers. Enter what you WROTE, not what you wish you wrote — the misses are the valuable part.

cards.def:
**Paper first. App second. Enter what you actually answered.**
• The quiz here is the same 30 questions, same numbers, same letters.
• A miss here is a gift: it gets a walkthrough now and comes back on the review ladder later.
• No clock on this unit — it is a grader, not a race.
cards.hint: The goal of a study guide is finding the holes BEFORE the test does.

cards.def:
**Each rule applies only over its own listed interval — find which interval x falls in, then use that rule.**
• Boundary points matter: check whether the interval is open (<) or closed (≤) at the exact value you're evaluating.
• A function can only use ONE rule per input — never average or combine two pieces.
cards.hint: Find the right interval FIRST, evaluate second — never the other way around.

cards.term: Absolute value as a piecewise function
cards.def:
**|expression| splits into two pieces at the value that makes the expression 0.**
• Where the inside is ≥ 0, the rule is just the expression itself.
• Where the inside is < 0, the rule is the expression's opposite (multiply by −1).
cards.hint: Find the zero of the inside expression first — that's where the split happens.

cards.def:
**A function that stays constant across each interval, then jumps to a new value at the next.**
• The domain is every x-value across all the intervals combined.
• The range is just the LIST of output values used — repeats don't count twice, and values between steps are never included.
cards.hint: Range of a step function is a short list of numbers, not a continuous interval.

cards.def:
**Recursive defines each term from the one before it; explicit defines any term directly from its position.**
• Recursive: aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + d (or aₙ₋₁ − |d|, however it's phrased) — you need the previous term to find the next.
• Explicit: aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d — jump straight to any term without finding the ones before it.
cards.hint: Explicit is the one you actually want for "find the 50th term" — recursive would take 49 steps.

cards.term: Sum of a finite arithmetic series
cards.def:
**Sₙ = n/2 · (a₁ + aₙ) — average the first and last term, then multiply by how many terms there are.**
• You need the LAST term before you can use this formula — find it with the explicit formula first if it isn't given.
• This works no matter how many terms there are, as long as the series is arithmetic (constant common difference).
cards.hint: Find the last term first if you don't already have it — the sum formula needs both ends.

cards.def:
**Σ (read "sigma") sums up an expression as n runs from the lower limit to the upper limit, one integer at a time.**
• Matching a series to its sigma notation means checking BOTH the formula inside AND the limits above and below.
• A correct-looking formula with the wrong limits describes a different series entirely — always check both.
cards.hint: Two things can be wrong in sigma notation: the formula, or the limits — check both separately.

cards.def:
**Split into two cases — the inside equals the other side, or the inside's OPPOSITE equals the other side — then solve each.**
• |A| = B splits into A = B and A = −B.
• Check each candidate solution back in the ORIGINAL equation — absolute value equations can sometimes produce an extra solution that doesn't actually work.
cards.hint: Two cases, two equations, two candidate answers — always check both back in the original.

cards.term: Solving a quadratic inequality by graphing
cards.def:
**Find where the parabola equals 0 first — those boundary points split the number line into the regions the inequality asks about.**
• A picture of the parabola (or knowing which way it opens) tells you which region satisfies "greater than" versus "less than".
• A downward-opening parabola is positive BETWEEN its zeros and negative outside them — an upward one is the reverse.
cards.hint: Zeros first, direction of opening second — those two facts alone answer the inequality.

questions.q: SG #1 (adapted — the paper asks you to graph this) — For f(x) = 6 when −8 ≤ x < 1, f(x) = −2x when 1 ≤ x < 8, and f(x) = −2 + x when 8 ≤ x ≤ 16, what is f(5)?
questions.hint: Find which interval 5 falls in before evaluating anything.
steps: 5 falls in the interval 1 ≤ x < 8, so use the rule f(x) = −2x for this input.

ex.main: **−10.** The interval, not the numbering of the pieces, decides which rule applies.

variant.q: For g(x) = 9 when −6 ≤ x < 0, g(x) = −3x when 0 ≤ x < 6, and g(x) = −3 + x when 6 ≤ x ≤ 14, what is g(4)?
variant.hint: Find which interval 4 falls in before evaluating anything.
steps: 4 falls in the interval 0 ≤ x < 6, so use the rule g(x) = −3x.

questions.q: SG #2 (adapted — the paper shows a graph to match) — A piecewise function is defined by −6 for −10 < x ≤ 2, 2x for 2 < x < 8, and −x + 2 for 8 ≤ x < 16. What is the function's value at exactly x = 2?
questions.hint: Check which interval's inequality actually includes x = 2 — pay attention to < versus ≤.
steps: The first piece is defined on −10 < x ≤ 2 — this interval INCLUDES x = 2, since it uses ≤.
The second piece is defined on 2 < x < 8, which does NOT include x = 2, since it uses strict <.
So the correct rule at x = 2 is the first one: f(2) = −6.

ex.main: **−6.** This is exactly the skill a graph's open vs. closed circles are testing — which piece owns the shared boundary point.

variant.q: A piecewise function is defined by −8 for −12 < x ≤ 3, 3x for 3 < x < 9, and −x + 5 for 9 ≤ x < 18. What is the function's value at exactly x = 3?
variant.hint: Check which interval's inequality actually includes x = 3.
steps: The first piece, −12 < x ≤ 3, includes x = 3 because it uses ≤.
The second piece, 3 < x < 9, does not include x = 3, since it's a strict inequality.
So h(3) = −8, using the first piece.

questions.q: SG #3 — Which shows f(x) = |2x − 12| expressed as a piecewise-defined function?
questions.hint: Find where the inside expression, 2x − 12, equals 0 — that's the split point.
steps: Find the zero of the inside expression: 2x − 12 = 0, so x = 6.
Where 2x − 12 ≥ 0 (that is, x ≥ 6), the absolute value just keeps the expression as-is: 2x − 12.
Where 2x − 12 < 0 (x < 6), the absolute value flips its sign: −(2x − 12) = −2x + 12.

ex.main: **2x − 12 for x ≥ 6; −2x + 12 for x < 6.** The split always happens exactly at the zero of the inside expression.

variant.q: Which shows f(x) = |4x − 20| expressed as a piecewise-defined function?
variant.hint: Find where 4x − 20 equals 0.
steps: Set the inside expression to 0: 4x − 20 = 0, so x = 5.

questions.q: SG #4 (adapted — the paper also asks you to graph this) — A bike rental hub charges $20 for 0 < x ≤ 6 hours, $30 for 6 < x ≤ 12 hours, $40 for 12 < x ≤ 18 hours, and $50 for 18 < x ≤ 24 hours. What are the range and the maximum value of this step function?
questions.hint: The range of a step function is the short LIST of actual output values used, not everything in between.
steps: The function only ever outputs 20, 30, 40, or 50 — never anything in between, so the range is the list {20, 30, 40, 50}, not a continuous interval.
The largest of those output values is 50.
So the range is {20, 30, 40, 50} and the maximum is 50.

ex.main: **Range {20, 30, 40, 50}; maximum 50.** A step function's range is a finite list of the values it actually takes — the gaps between steps are never included.

variant.q: A parking garage charges $8 for 0 < x ≤ 4 hours, $14 for 4 < x ≤ 8 hours, $20 for 8 < x ≤ 12 hours, and $26 for 12 < x ≤ 16 hours. What are the range and the maximum value of this step function?
variant.hint: List the actual dollar amounts charged — that list IS the range.
steps: The four possible charges are 8, 14, 20, and 26 — nothing in between is ever charged.
So the range is the list {8, 14, 20, 26}.
The maximum of that list is 26.

questions.q: SG #5 — Find the 2nd and 3rd terms of the sequence −7, ___, ___, −22, −27, …
questions.hint: Find the common difference from the two terms you DO know, −22 and −27.
steps: The 4th and 5th terms are −22 and −27, so the common difference is −27 − (−22) = −5.
Working backward with d = −5: the 2nd term is −7 + (−5) = −12.

ex.main: **−12, −17.** Finding d from the terms you're given, even if they aren't adjacent to the ones you need, is the way into this problem.

variant.q: Find the 2nd and 3rd terms of the sequence −9, ___, ___, −27, −33, …
variant.hint: Find the common difference from the two terms you already know.
steps: The 4th and 5th terms are −27 and −33, so d = −33 − (−27) = −6.

questions.q: SG #6 — Find the missing term of the arithmetic sequence 26, ___, 18, …
questions.hint: In an arithmetic sequence, a missing middle term is the average of its neighbors.
steps: The missing term sits exactly halfway between 26 and 18 in an arithmetic sequence.

ex.main: **22.** The middle term of any three consecutive arithmetic terms is always the average of the other two.

variant.q: Find the missing term of the arithmetic sequence 31, ___, 15, …
variant.hint: Average the two known terms.
steps: The missing middle term is the average of its neighbors.

questions.q: SG #7 — Find the arithmetic mean aₙ of aₙ₋₁ = 3.9 and aₙ₊₁ = 7.1.
questions.hint: The arithmetic mean of two numbers is just their average.
steps: The term between two arithmetic-sequence neighbors is their average.

ex.main: **5.5.** "Arithmetic mean" between two sequence terms is exactly the same idea as the missing-middle-term problems — just different wording.

variant.q: Find the arithmetic mean aₙ of aₙ₋₁ = 2.4 and aₙ₊₁ = 9.8.
variant.hint: Average the two given values.

questions.q: SG #8 — Is the sequence 13, 20, 27, 34, … arithmetic? If so, identify the common difference.
questions.hint: Check whether the difference between EVERY consecutive pair is the same.
steps: Every gap is the same value, 7.
So the sequence is arithmetic, with common difference 7.

ex.main: **Yes; 7.** Checking more than one gap matters — a single matching pair could be a coincidence.

variant.q: Is the sequence 11, 18, 25, 32, … arithmetic? If so, identify the common difference.
variant.hint: Check the gaps between every consecutive pair.
steps: So it's arithmetic with common difference 7.

questions.q: SG #9 — Is the sequence 14, 21, 42, 77, … arithmetic? If so, identify the common difference.
questions.hint: Check ALL the gaps, not just the first one.
steps: Check the second gap: 42 − 21 = 21 — this does NOT match the first gap.
Since the gaps aren't constant, the sequence is not arithmetic.

ex.main: **No.** The first gap alone (7) looks promising, which is exactly why checking only one gap is a trap.

variant.q: Is the sequence 9, 18, 36, 63, … arithmetic? If so, identify the common difference.
variant.hint: Check every gap, not just the first.
steps: The gaps aren't constant, so it isn't arithmetic.

questions.q: SG #10 — Is the sequence −2.4, 9.8, 22, 34.2, … arithmetic? If so, identify the common difference.
questions.hint: Compute the gaps carefully with the decimals.
steps: 34.2 − 22 = 12.2. All three gaps match, so it's arithmetic with common difference 12.2.

variant.q: Is the sequence −3.6, 7.4, 18.4, 29.4, … arithmetic? If so, identify the common difference.
variant.hint: Compute each gap carefully.
steps: 29.4 − 18.4 = 11.0. All match, so it's arithmetic with common difference 11.

questions.q: SG #11 — Find the 50th term of the sequence 5, −2, −9, −16, …
questions.hint: Find a1 and d, then use the explicit formula rather than counting by hand.
steps: a1 = 5, and the common difference is −2 − 5 = −7.
Use the explicit formula: a50 = a1 + (50 − 1)d = 5 + 49(−7).

variant.q: Find the 60th term of the sequence 8, 2, −4, −10, …
variant.hint: Find a1 and d, then use the explicit formula.

questions.q: SG #12 — Find the 110th term of the sequence −7, 3, 13, 23, …
questions.hint: Find a1 and d first.

variant.q: Find the 120th term of the sequence −9, 2, 13, 24, …
variant.hint: Find a1 and d first.

questions.q: SG #13 — For the recursive definition aₙ = 45 when n = 1, and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ − 5 when n > 1, what is the explicit definition?
questions.hint: Identify a1 and d from the recursive rule, then plug into the standard explicit form.
steps: The recursive rule starts at a1 = 45 and subtracts 5 each step, so d = −5.
The explicit form is always aₙ = a1 + (n − 1)d.

ex.main: **aₙ = 45 − 5(n − 1).** Every recursive rule of this shape converts the same way — read off a1 and d, then drop them into the explicit template.

variant.q: For the recursive definition aₙ = 60 when n = 1, and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ − 8 when n > 1, what is the explicit definition?
variant.hint: Read off a1 and d, then use the explicit template.
steps: The explicit form is aₙ = a1 + (n − 1)d.

questions.q: SG #14 — Evaluate the series Σₙ₌₁⁸⁵ (2n + 6).
questions.hint: This is arithmetic — find the first term, the last term, and use the sum formula rather than adding 85 numbers by hand.
steps: The first term (n = 1) is 2(1) + 6 = 8. The last term (n = 85) is 2(85) + 6 = 176.

ex.main: **7,820.** Recognizing this as an arithmetic series turns 85 additions into one formula.

variant.q: Evaluate the series Σₙ₌₁⁶⁰ (3n + 2).
variant.hint: Find the first and last term, then use the sum formula.

questions.q: SG #15 — A grocery clerk sets up a triangular display of 12-pack cartons: 15 cartons at the base, one at the top, one fewer in each row above. How many cartons are needed for the complete display?
questions.hint: This is the sum of the arithmetic series 15 + 14 + 13 + … + 1.
steps: The rows go 15, 14, 13, …, down to 1 — an arithmetic series with a1 = 15, an = 1, and 15 terms.
Use the sum formula: S = n/2 · (a1 + an) = 15/2 · (15 + 1).

ex.main: **120 cartons.** A triangular stack is always the sum of consecutive counting numbers, which the arithmetic series formula handles directly.

variant.q: A display is set up with 12 cartons at the base, one at the top, one fewer in each row above. How many cartons are needed?
variant.hint: Sum the series 12 + 11 + … + 1.
steps: The rows are 12, 11, …, 1 — 12 terms, a1 = 12, an = 1.

ex.main: **78 cartons.**

questions.q: SG #16 (adapted — the paper asks for a written explanation) — The number of sit-ups Marla does each day is 17, 21, 25, 29, 33 for Days 1 through 5. At this rate, how many sit-ups will she do on Day 12?
questions.hint: Find a1 and d from the given days, then use the explicit formula for Day 12.
steps: a1 = 17 (Day 1), and the common difference is 21 − 17 = 4.
Explicit formula: aₙ = a1 + (n − 1)d, so a12 = 17 + (12 − 1)(4).

ex.main: **61.** The explicit formula reaches Day 12 in one step, without needing Days 6 through 11 at all.

variant.q: The number of push-ups Marcus does each day is 22, 27, 32, 37, 42 for Days 1 through 5. At this rate, how many push-ups will he do on Day 10?
variant.hint: Find a1 and d, then use the explicit formula for Day 10.

questions.q: SG #17 — What is the sum of the finite arithmetic series 7.6 + 6.3 + 5 + 3.7 + 2.4 + 1.1 + (−0.2) + (−1.5)?
questions.hint: Use the sum formula rather than adding eight decimals by hand.
steps: There are 8 terms, from a1 = 7.6 to a8 = −1.5.

variant.q: What is the sum of the finite arithmetic series 9.2 + 7.5 + 5.8 + 4.1 + 2.4 + 0.7 + (−1.0) + (−2.7)?
variant.hint: Use the sum formula with the first and last terms.
steps: There are 8 terms, a1 = 9.2 and a8 = −2.7.

questions.q: SG #18 — What is the sum of the finite arithmetic series 29 + 32 + 35 + 38 + 41 + … + 59?
questions.hint: Find how many terms there are first — you'll need it for the sum formula.
steps: d = 3, a1 = 29, and the last term is 59. Find n: 59 = 29 + (n − 1)(3), so n − 1 = 10, meaning n = 11.

ex.main: **484.** Finding the number of terms is the step most easily skipped, and the formula doesn't work without it.

variant.q: What is the sum of the finite arithmetic series 18 + 22 + 26 + 30 + 34 + … + 58?
variant.hint: Find the number of terms first.

questions.q: SG #19 — What is the sum of the finite arithmetic series (−5) + 0 + 5 + 10 + … + 65?
questions.hint: Find the number of terms using d = 5.

variant.q: What is the sum of the finite arithmetic series (−8) + (−2) + 4 + 10 + … + 58?
variant.hint: Find the number of terms using d = 6.

questions.q: SG #20 — What is the sum of the finite arithmetic series 26 + 29 + 32 + 35 + 38 + 41 + 44?
questions.hint: There are exactly 7 terms listed — use the sum formula directly.
steps: a1 = 26, an = 44, and there are 7 terms.

variant.q: What is the sum of the finite arithmetic series 14 + 18 + 22 + 26 + 30 + 34 + 38?
variant.hint: There are 7 terms — use the sum formula.

questions.q: SG #21 — A projectile's distance traveled each second, starting with the first second, follows the arithmetic sequence 26, 44, 62, 80, … (in feet). Find the total distance traveled in seven seconds.
questions.hint: You need the sum of the first 7 terms, not just the 7th term itself.
steps: a1 = 26, d = 18. The question asks for total distance, which is a SUM, not a single term.

ex.main: **560 feet.** "Total distance" is a strong signal this is a sum question, not a single-term question — reading that correctly is half the problem.

variant.q: A different projectile's distance traveled each second follows the sequence 15, 29, 43, 57, … (in feet). Find the total distance traveled in seven seconds.
variant.hint: Find the sum of the first 7 terms.

questions.q: SG #22 (adapted — the paper asks for two written explanations) — A necklace has 18 rows of beads, with the number of beads per row given by the series 3 + 10 + 17 + 24 + … What is the total number of beads in the necklace?
questions.hint: Find the 18th term first, then use the sum formula.
steps: Use the sum formula: S = n/2 · (a1 + an) = 18/2 · (3 + 122).

ex.main: **1,125 beads.** This is exactly the same two-step pattern as every other series sum here: find the last term, then average the two ends and multiply by the count.

variant.q: A necklace has 16 rows of beads, with the number per row given by the series 5 + 12 + 19 + 26 + … What is the total number of beads?
variant.hint: Find the 16th term first, then use the sum formula.

questions.q: SG #23 — Use sigma notation to write the series 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + … for 10 terms.
questions.hint: Check that the formula produces the right FIRST few terms, and that the limits give the right COUNT of terms.
steps: Test the formula 2n at n = 1, 2, 3: gives 2, 4, 6 — matches the series exactly.
Check the limits: n = 1 to 10 gives exactly 10 terms, matching "for 10 terms".
Σₙ₌₀¹⁰ 2n would give 11 terms (n = 0 through 10) — one too many, so that option is wrong despite the right formula.

ex.main: **Σₙ₌₁¹⁰ 2n.** Both the formula AND the limits have to be checked — a correct formula with the wrong limits describes a different series.

variant.q: Use sigma notation to write the series 3 + 6 + 9 + 12 + … for 8 terms.
variant.hint: Test the formula against the first few terms, then check the term count from the limits.
steps: Σₙ₌₀⁸ 3n would give 9 terms — too many.

ex.main: **Σₙ₌₁⁸ 3n.**

questions.q: SG #24 — Use sigma notation to write the series 6.6 + 15.4 + 24.2 + … for 5 terms.
questions.hint: Find the common difference first, then build the formula from a1 and d.
steps: The common difference is 15.4 − 6.6 = 8.8, so the formula has the shape (something) + 8.8n.
Test n = 1: it must give 6.6, so (something) + 8.8 = 6.6, meaning (something) = −2.2. Formula: −2.2 + 8.8n.
Check the limits: n = 1 to 5 gives 5 terms, matching "for 5 terms".

variant.q: Use sigma notation to write the series 4.5 + 12.5 + 20.5 + … for 6 terms.
variant.hint: Find d, then find the constant that makes n = 1 give the right first term.
steps: d = 12.5 − 4.5 = 8, so the formula has the shape (something) + 8n.
n = 1 to 6 gives 6 terms, matching the count.

questions.q: SG #25 — Use sigma notation to write the series 49 + 54 + 59 + … for 14 terms.
questions.hint: Find the formula from d and the first term, then check the limits give 14 terms.
steps: d = 54 − 49 = 5, so the formula is (something) + 5n. At n = 1: (something) + 5 = 49, so (something) = 44.
Formula: 44 + 5n. Check: n = 1 gives 44 + 5 = 49 ✓, n = 2 gives 44 + 10 = 54 ✓.
The limits n = 1 to 14 give exactly 14 terms, matching "for 14 terms".

variant.q: Use sigma notation to write the series 33 + 39 + 45 + … for 12 terms.
variant.hint: Find d, then the constant, then check the limits.
steps: d = 39 − 33 = 6, formula shape (something) + 6n. At n = 1: (something) + 6 = 33, so (something) = 27.

questions.q: SG #26 — Evaluate the series Σₙ₌₃⁸ 5n.
questions.hint: The sum starts at n = 3, not n = 1 — don't include the missing early terms.
steps: List the terms from n = 3 to n = 8: 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40 — six terms total.
This is an arithmetic series: a1 = 15, an = 40, n = 6 terms.

ex.main: **165.** The lower limit starting above 1 is easy to miss — always list out (or count) exactly which terms are actually included.

variant.q: Evaluate the series Σₙ₌₂⁷ 4n.
variant.hint: The sum starts at n = 2, not n = 1.
steps: Terms from n = 2 to n = 7: 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28 — six terms.

questions.q: SG #27 — Evaluate the series Σₙ₌₁⁴ (n + 4).
questions.hint: List out all four terms and add them.

ex.main: **26.** With only 4 terms, listing them out directly is faster than reaching for the sum formula.

variant.q: Evaluate the series Σₙ₌₁⁵ (n + 3).
variant.hint: List all five terms and add them.
steps: At n = 1 through 5: the terms are 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.

questions.q: SG #28 — Use a calculator to evaluate the series Σₙ₌₁⁵⁰ (n² − 2).
questions.hint: This series isn't arithmetic (it has an n² term), so the arithmetic sum formula doesn't apply — this one genuinely needs direct computation.
steps: Σn² for n = 1 to 50 uses the sum-of-squares formula, and the −2 is subtracted once per term (50 times total).
Σₙ₌₁⁵⁰ n² = 42,925. Subtracting 2 for each of the 50 terms: 42,925 − 100.

ex.main: **42,825.** Not every series here is arithmetic — an n² term is the signal that the sum formula from the other questions doesn't apply.

variant.q: Use a calculator to evaluate the series Σₙ₌₁⁴⁰ (n² − 3).
variant.hint: Use the sum-of-squares total for n = 1 to 40, then subtract 3 once per term.
steps: Subtract 3 for each of the 40 terms: 22,140 − 120.

questions.q: SG #29 — Find the solution of the equation −x + 3 = |3x + 9|.
questions.hint: Split the absolute value into two cases, then check each candidate solution back in the original equation.
steps: Both candidates check out in the original equation, so both are genuine solutions: x = −1.5 and x = −6.

ex.main: **−1.5 and −6.** Both cases of an absolute value equation need to be checked back in the ORIGINAL equation — here, both happen to hold up.

variant.q: Find the solution of the equation −x + 5 = |2x + 10|.
variant.hint: Split into two cases and check each candidate in the original equation.
steps: Both check out: x ≈ −1.67 and x = −15.

questions.q: SG #30 — What is the solution of the inequality −x² + 16 > 0?
questions.hint: Find where −x² + 16 equals 0 first — those are the boundary points.
steps: Find the zeros: −x² + 16 = 0, so x² = 16, giving x = −4 or x = 4.
The graph of y = −x² + 16 is a downward-opening parabola (the leading coefficient is negative).
A downward-opening parabola is positive BETWEEN its zeros, so the solution is −4 < x < 4.

ex.main: **−4 < x < 4.** A downward-opening parabola sits above the x-axis between its two zeros and below it outside them — the opposite of an upward one.

variant.q: What is the solution of the inequality −x² + 25 > 0?
variant.hint: Find the zeros first, then use the fact that this parabola opens downward.
steps: Zeros: −x² + 25 = 0, so x² = 25, x = −5 or x = 5.
The parabola opens downward (negative leading coefficient).
It's positive between its zeros: −5 < x < 5.
